readings.title: 'Brutal' toll of war on Dubai's tourist trade
body: 2 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Sameer Hashmi Last year Dubai welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally, but the US-Israel war with Iran has had a devastating impact on visitor numbers, and local businesses are struggling. On most evenings, Dubai's restaurants would usually be packed, with the constant buzz of diners, of tourists and residents filling tables across the city. But over the past month, many of those tables have sat empty. For Natasha Sideris, the shift has been sudden and stark. She opened her first restaurant in Dubai in 2014. Over the past decade, her Tashas hospitality group has grown to 14 outlets across the country, employing more than 1,000 people. But the US-Israel war with Iran is now taking a heavy toll on her business. Sideris says many of her restaurants, which are popular with both residents and expats, have seen revenues fall by more than 50%. But outlets that depend heavily on tourists have been hit much harder, with declines of 70% to 80%. The crisis has forced her to cut salaries by 30% for all staff including herself. "The current situation is brutal," she says. "I had a choice – either fire 30% of my staff or cut salaries to save jobs. I chose the latter for now." Sideris adds that the impact would have been worse if many of her outlets were not located inside community malls and close to residential neighbourhoods, where they still rely on local customers. The current tough reality is playing out across much of Dubai's restaurant sector. One senior executive at a restaurant chain, who asked not to be named, said footfall at its outlets has dropped to just 15-20% of normal, forcing them to place more than half of staff on unpaid leave. "We have no option," he says. "We've already shut down a few outlets temporarily, and the rest are operating with minimal staff." The impact is not limited to restaurants. The entire tourism ecosystem – from hotels and travel agencies, to transport companies and airlines – is feeling the strain. Over the past two decades, Dubai has built itself into one of the world's leading tourism hubs. Last year, the emirate welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally. But since the war began, that momentum has been sharply disrupted. The wider UAE has come under repeated attacks, with Dubai among the key targets of Iran's military response following US and Israeli strikes. Authorities say more than 2,400 missiles and drones have been launched towards the UAE, targeting airports, ports and civilian areas, including hotels and residential buildings. More than 90% of them were intercepted and destroyed, officials say. But some debris has fallen across parts of Dubai, including major residential areas, hotels and the airport. Images of fragments striking the Fairmont hotel on the upscale Palm Island were circulated widely online. To date, 11 people have been killed and more than 185 injured across the UAE, according to authorities in the country. The conflict, which began on 28 February, has disrupted air travel across the region. In the early weeks, tens of thousands of visitors were stranded before being evacuated on special flights. Thousands of regular, scheduled flights have been cancelled since the conflict began, bringing one of the region's busiest travel hubs to a halt at times. Dubai International Airport – the world's busiest for international passengers – handled 95.2 million travellers last year.  Some operations have since resumed, with flag-carrier Emirates operating a reduced flight schedule while working to restore full network operations. But with tourists leaving and the number of new arrivals collapsing, hotel stays in Dubai have fallen steeply. Occupancy levels across Dubai hotels dropped to between 15% and 20% of the usual level for this time of the year in the weeks following the outbreak of the war, according to Mamoun Hmiden, chief business officer at travel booking firm Wego. Hotels have responded with deep discounts, particularly during the Eid period, in an attempt to attract residents. Some luxury properties on Palm Jumeirah, one of the city's premium hotel hubs, have cut prices by as much as half. "The uncertainty is disrupting everyone at the moment," says Hmiden. Some hospitality chains have temporarily shut down some properties or closed certain sections, citing scheduled renovations – a move typically seen during the quieter summer months. A senior executive at an international hospitality group said occupancy at some properties had fallen to single digits. "It made sense to cut operational costs by shutting down for a few weeks and reviewing the situation later," he says. Even business hotels are under pressure. Dubai, a major hub for conferences and events, has seen organisers cancel or postpone large gatherings in the coming months. Majestic Hotels, which operates around 450 rooms across three properties, says occupancy has dropped to record lows. "We are seeing cancellations beyond April," says Varun Raj, cluster director of sales and marketing. "A lot of events have been cancelled, making it difficult for travellers to plan ahead." The slowdown comes after several years of rapid growth. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Dubai was among the first destinations to reopen to international visitors, allowing its tourism sector to recover faster than many global peers. Since then, it has expanded into a broader and more diversified market – strengthening its position as a luxury destination, while also attracting large numbers of mid-market and price-sensitive travellers from regions such as South Asia, Europe and the former Soviet states. That surge in demand has been matched by a sharp increase in supply. Years of growth have driven expansion not only in hotel capacity, but also in short-term apartment rentals across the city. That additional supply is now under pressure. Data firm AirDNA shared that a little over 226,500 short-term bookings were cancelled across the UAE between February 28 to March 29, the first month since the war began.   The downturn is also being felt by the migrant workforce that form the backbone of Dubai's hospitality industry – from restaurant staff to hotel workers.  As demand weakens, many have seen their hours reduced, or they have been placed on unpaid leave. While the UAE's labour system allows companies to adjust quickly to changing conditions, that flexibility can leave workers exposed to sudden income losses. "It feels like we are back to the Covid-19 period," says a South Asian waiter working at a high-end restaurant. There are fears we could lose our jobs again and be forced to go back home." He and several colleagues have been placed on unpaid leave, with no clarity on when – or if – they will return to work. Some hotels, including five-star properties, have started laying off employees. Rights groups say many migrant workers in the UAE are already financially vulnerable, with some carrying debt linked to recruitment fees. The impact of the war is also being felt across the wider Middle East. Research by Tourism Economics, part of Oxford Economics, suggests that between 23 million and 38 million fewer people could travel to the region this year, depending on how long the conflict continues. Between $34bn (£25bn) and $56bn in visitor spending could be lost. "If the war ends soon, there could be a quick recovery," says Hmiden. "But if it drags on, we have to start questioning the entire summer season." This week – Dubai announced $272.26 million in support for businesses, including tourism, over the next three to six months. Hotels will be allowed to delay sales-related fees and tourism dirham charges – a fee applied to guests staying in the city.  Authorities in Dubai are also working on plans to revive tourism once the conflict subsides, including new campaigns and promotional offers.  "The war is out of our control," says one official. "But we are preparing for when it ends." More like this: • How the Iran war is affecting global travel • How a prolonged Middle East conflict could reshape how we fly • Is Dubai's glossy image under threat? Sideris is hoping that landlords will provide rent relief in the form of deferred payments or reduced payments for the time being to support local businesses. For Sideris, the outlook remains uncertain. She says a recovery is possible from October if the war ends soon. But if the conflict continues, the timeline could shift to next year – bringing the risk of layoffs and outlet closures. "We've got enough cash to see us through a month or two... maximum three, and then past that, what do we do? After that, we will have to take tougher calls. Hopefully not. And this insanity ends soon." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. 去年迪拜接待了1959万国际游客，使其成为全球到访量最大的城市之一，但美国-以色列与伊朗的战争对游客数量造成了毁灭性影响，当地企业正艰难挣扎。在大多数夜晚，迪拜的餐厅通常会座无虚席，食客和游客的持续喧嚣声填满全城的餐桌。但在过去一个月里，许多餐桌一直空着。

对Natasha Sideris来说，这种转变来得突然而剧烈。她于2014年在迪拜开了第一家餐厅。过去十年间，她的Tashas餐饮集团已发展到全国14家门店，雇佣超过1000名员工。但美国-以色列与伊朗的战争现在正对她的生意造成沉重打击。Sideris表示，她许多深受本地居民和外籍人士欢迎的餐厅，收入下降了超过50%。而严重依赖游客的门店受到的冲击更大，跌幅达70%至80%。这场危机迫使她将所有员工（包括她自己）的薪资削减30%。她说：“当前形势非常残酷。我面临一个选择——要么解雇30%的员工，要么削减薪资以保住工作岗位。我暂时选择了后者。”

Sideris补充说，如果她的许多门店不是设在社区商场内、靠近居民区，影响会更大，因为这些门店仍依赖本地顾客。当前严峻的现实正在迪拜大部分餐饮行业上演。一家连锁餐厅的高级高管（要求匿名）表示，其门店客流量已降至正常水平的仅15%至20%，迫使他们让超过一半的员工无薪休假。他说：“我们别无选择。我们已经暂时关闭了几家门店，其余门店以最少人员运营。”

影响不仅限于餐饮业。整个旅游生态系统——从酒店和旅行社，到运输公司和航空公司——都感受到压力。过去二十年来，迪拜已将自身打造成全球领先的旅游枢纽之一。去年，这个酋长国接待了1959万国际游客，使其成为全球到访量最大的城市之一。但自战争爆发以来，这一势头被严重打断。更广泛的阿联酋遭受了反复攻击，迪拜是美国和以色列打击后伊朗军事回应的主要目标之一。当局表示，超过2400枚导弹和无人机被射向阿联酋，目标是机场、港口和民用区域，包括酒店和住宅建筑。官员称其中90%以上被拦截并摧毁。但一些碎片已落在迪拜部分地区，包括

主要住宅区、酒店和机场。碎片击中高档棕榈岛费尔蒙酒店的画面在网上广泛传播。据阿联酋当局称，截至目前，全国已有11人死亡，超过185人受伤。这场始于2月28日的冲突，已扰乱整个地区的航空旅行。冲突初期，数万名游客被困，随后通过专机撤离。自冲突爆发以来，数千架次定期航班被取消，一度使该地区最繁忙的旅行枢纽之一陷入停滞。迪拜国际机场——全球国际旅客吞吐量最大的机场——去年接待了9520万人次旅客。部分运营现已恢复，旗舰航空公司阿联酋航空在努力恢复全面网络运营的同时，维持着缩减的航班时刻表。但随着游客离去和新 arrivals 数量骤降，迪拜的酒店入住率急剧下滑。据旅行预订公司Wego的首席商务官Mamoun Hmiden称，战争爆发后的几周内，迪拜各酒店的入住率降至往年同期正常水平的15%至20%。酒店纷纷推出大幅折扣，尤其是在开斋节期间，以吸引本地居民。朱美拉棕榈岛——该市高端酒店集中地之一——部分豪华物业的房价已下调近一半。“目前，不确定性正扰乱着每个人，”Hmiden表示。部分酒店连锁以计划中的翻修为由，暂时关闭了某些物业或部分区域——此举通常在较为冷清的夏季出现。一家国际酒店集团的高级高管表示，部分物业的入住率已降至个位数。“关闭几周以削减运营成本，稍后再评估情况，这样是合理的，”他说。即便是商务酒店也承压。迪拜是会议和活动的重要枢纽，但近期已看到组织者取消或推迟未来数月的大型聚会。Majestic Hotels在三个物业运营约450间客房，其表示入住率已降至历史低点。“我们看到4月之后的取消订单，”销售与市场营销集群总监Varun Raj说。“大量活动被取消，令旅行者难以提前规划。”此次放缓发生在数年快速增长之后。新冠疫情期间，迪拜是最早向国际游客重新开放的目的地之一，使其旅游业比许多全球同行恢复得更快。此后，它已扩展为更广泛、更多元化的市场——巩固了其作为豪华目的地的地位，同时

同时也吸引了大量来自南亚、欧洲和前苏联国家的中端市场和价格敏感型旅客。需求的激增伴随着供应的急剧增加。多年的增长不仅推动了酒店容量的扩张，也促进了该市短期公寓租赁的发展。这部分新增供应现在面临压力。数据公司AirDNA分享称，在2月28日至3月29日期间（战争开始后的第一个月），阿联酋各地约有22.65万笔短期预订被取消。经济下滑也影响到了构成迪拜酒店业支柱的移民劳动力——从餐厅员工到酒店工作人员。随着需求减弱，许多人工作时间被减少，或被安排无薪休假。虽然阿联酋的劳工制度允许企业快速适应变化的条件，但这种灵活性可能使工人面临突如其来的收入损失。“感觉我们回到了新冠疫情期间，”一位在高档餐厅工作的南亚服务员说，“我们担心会再次失业，被迫回国。”他和几位同事已被安排无薪休假，不清楚何时或能否重返工作岗位。一些酒店，包括五星级酒店，已开始裁员。权利团体表示，阿联酋许多移民工人经济上本已脆弱，有些人背负着与招聘费相关的债务。战争的影响也波及整个中东地区。牛津经济研究院旗下旅游经济公司的研究表明，根据冲突持续时间长短，今年该地区游客人数可能减少2300万至3800万，游客支出可能损失340亿至560亿美元。“如果战争很快结束，可能会快速复苏，”赫米登说，“但如果拖下去，我们不得不开始质疑整个夏季旅游季。”本周，迪拜宣布在未来三至六个月内为包括旅游业在内的企业提供2.7226亿美元的支持。酒店将被允许延期支付销售相关费用和旅游迪拉姆费用——这项费用适用于入住该市的客人。迪拜当局也在制定计划，一旦冲突平息就重振旅游业，包括新的宣传活动和促销优惠。“战争超出了我们的控制，”一位官员说，“但我们正在为战争结束做准备。”更多相关内容：• 伊朗战争如何影响全球旅行• 持久的中东冲突如何重塑我们的飞行方式• 迪拜的光鲜形象是否受到威胁？西德里希望房东能提供租金减免，以延期付款或减少当前租金的形式，支持当地企业。对于西……

deris，前景依然不确定。她表示，如果战争很快结束，复苏可能在十月出现。但若冲突持续，时间表可能推迟到明年——这带来裁员和门店关闭的风险。“我们有足够的现金维持一两个月……最多三个月，之后我们该怎么办？在那之后，我们将不得不做出更艰难的决定。希望不会如此，但愿这种疯狂尽快结束。”——如需获取面向董事会及其他高层的全球洞察和专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》新闻简报，而《基本清单》则提供精选的特稿和见解。欲了解更多商业及更广泛领域资讯，请关注我们的LinkedIn。商业 战争 新闻 特稿 伊朗 战争 商业世界

readings.title: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
body: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
What separates the very best in the world from the remaining 7 billion of us?

Exceptional talent often looks like an act of revolution — a person doing something in a way no one has ever done it before — but many revolutionary talents are actually built on a foundation of evolutionary tweaks. These tweaks develop over time, often compensating for weaknesses and anxieties that might derail a lesser talent.
For all his brilliance, though, Messi is famously anxious. For several years, he habitually vomited on the field before big matches.

Take the world’s best soccer player, an Argentinean named Lionel Messi. Messi has won more Ballon d’Or trophies, awarded to the best soccer player of the year, than any other player. He has scored more goals in a calendar year than any other living player, is the top all-time scorer in Spain’s La Liga, and has the highest goal ratio in the sport today, scoring almost once every match.

For all his brilliance, though, he’s famously anxious. For several years, Messi habitually vomited on the field before big matches. After a string of disappointing national-team losses, another former Argentinean giant of the game, the late Diego Maradona, uncharitably criticized Messi by suggesting that it was “useless trying to make a leader out of a man who goes to the toilet twenty times before a game.”

Being incredibly talented doesn’t immunize you against anxiety, and many of the world’s best grapple with anxiety precisely because they expect so much from themselves. But Messi hasn’t allowed his anxiety to diminish his brilliance because he’s mastered a coping mechanism that also doubles as the secret behind his tactical brilliance.
Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Second, he scopes out the opposition.

A soccer match runs for 90 minutes (plus a few minutes for “injury time”), and most players are active in the game from the first minute. As soon as the whistle blows, they implore their teammates to pass the ball and pursue the tactics their coaches laid out before the game.

But Messi is famous for not playing the game during its opening minutes. This is his evolutionary tweak, which developed as he played the game at progressively higher levels. For the opening minutes, Messi ambles back and forth near the middle of the field and almost never engages with his teammates. Whereas other players run and sometimes sprint, Messi spends much of his time walking, rarely breaking into more than a slow jog.

Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Easing into the game is Messi’s way of ensuring he’s fully engaged for the remainder of the game. His on-field vomiting has resolved itself, in part perhaps because he’s found a more effective way to calm his nerves. Second, he spends this time scoping out the opposition. His legs move slowly, but his eyes dart from player to player, assessing his opponents’ strengths, weaknesses, and tactics, and monitoring his own team’s movement with and around the ball. Messi is less valuable to his team early in the game, but this tactical pause elevates his value for the remaining 95 percent of the game.

If you split soccer game play into “preparatory” and “engaged” components, Messi leans heavily on preparation. During one classic game between Messi’s Barcelona and archrivals Real Madrid, in 2017, Messi ran for just four minutes and walked for more than eighty of the game’s ninety minutes. When he was engaged, though, he was dynamic, creating nine chances, scoring one goal, and feeding the ball to a teammate who scored another goal.
As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act.

That pattern isn’t unusual for Messi, and it’s often in the biggest games that he accentuates his in-game preparation. That preparation also explains his ability to find himself in the right place at the right time, over and over. Though his positional play appears otherworldly, it isn’t a miracle; it’s that he’s learned, minute by minute, that a particular defender leaves a particular square of pitch uncovered or that two midfielders leave a small corner of the pitch open when they gravitate to the middle of the field.
The lesson for the rest of us is clear: When you’re anxious, whether in athletics or in life more broadly, pause. Slow down . Prepare.

As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act. Judson Brewer, a psychiatrist and neuroscientist, has spent much of his career thinking about how to do nothing.
About fifteen years ago, Brewer developed a mindfulness-based treatment for addiction.
His approach instructs addicts to resist the waves of anxiety during moments of craving by following the four steps of an approach that goes by the acronym RAIN:
I nvestigate your emotions and thoughts (e.g., “What is happening in my body now?”)
N ote what is happening from moment to moment.

Brewer has said that his approach was inspired by clinical psychologist Tara Brach’s . To test the approach, Brewer worked with smokers who were struggling to quit. Nicotine addiction is notoriously stubborn — more so than many harder drugs that produce stronger immediate responses in users.

Before unleashing the program on smokers, Brewer wanted to test the system on himself. The problem was “I was a nonsmoker,” Brewer wrote, “who needed to be able to relate to patients who felt as though their heads were going to explode unless they smoked.”

Nicotine has a half-life of around two hours, so to begin, smokers need to resist the urge to light up for two hours at a time. Brewer reasoned that smokers who could last two hours without a cigarette would cultivate new nonsmoking habits, extending those stretches till they no longer felt the urge to smoke at all.

He simulated these periods of resistance by learning to meditate for two-hour stretches without moving. During moments of restlessness, he followed the RAIN steps — recognize, allow, investigate, note — and if he moved his body, the clock would reset, and he’d have to start again.

This might sound easy, but two hours is a long time to sit still without entertainment. “Surprisingly it wasn’t the physical pain of not shifting for a long time that got me,” Brewer wrote. “It was the restlessness … Those cravings shouted, ‘Get up!’ ”
Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean.

For many months, Brewer would get close, then restlessness would defeat him. “Then one day,” he wrote, “I did it. I sat for the full two hours … Each subsequent sit got easier and easier because I had the confidence that it could be done. And I knew that my patients could quit smoking. They simply needed the proper tools.”

Brewer was right. His patients had been stuck, incapable of quitting one of the most addictive substances on earth. But when he ran study after study, pitting his RAIN mindfulness method against the most effective addiction treatment approaches of the day, his approach was more than twice as effective.

Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean. They were more than five times as likely to have shaken their addictions using an approach that essentially taught them to pause at the moment their bodies were most urgently driving them to act.

Of the four steps in Brewer’s RAIN approach, the second — allowing — is perhaps the most critical. Allowing an experience to wash over you sounds disarmingly easy because it doesn’t require you to do anything. But that’s exactly the point. It’s difficult because you’re forced to do nothing despite the urge to act.

##段落
处理焦虑的一个聪明方法——源自足球巨星莱昂内尔·梅西
2023年6月22日
/
亚当·阿尔特博士
Facebook
X

德博拉·斯皮尔曼

是什么将世界最顶尖的人才与其余70亿人区分开来？

非凡的才华往往看起来像一场革命——一个人以从未有人做过的方式做事——但许多革命性的才华实际上建立在渐进式微调的基础上。这些微调随着时间发展，常常用来弥补那些可能让 lesser 天赋者偏离轨道的弱点和焦虑。

尽管梅西才华横溢，但他以焦虑著称。有几年，他在重大比赛前习惯性地在场上呕吐。

以世界最佳足球运动员、阿根廷人莱昂内尔·梅西为例。梅西赢得的金球奖（授予年度最佳足球运动员的奖项）比任何其他球员都多。他在一个日历年内打进的进球数超过任何其他现役球员，是西班牙西甲联赛的历史最佳射手，并且拥有当今最高的进球率，几乎每场比赛都能进球。

尽管他光芒四射，但他以焦虑闻名。有几年，梅西在大赛前习惯性地在球场上呕吐。在一连串令人失望的国家队失利之后，另一位已故的阿根廷足球巨匠迭戈·马拉多纳不客气地批评梅西，暗示“试图把一个赛前要上二十次厕所的人培养成领袖是没用的”。

拥有惊人的天赋并不能让你免受焦虑的侵袭，而世界上许多最优秀的人恰恰因为对自己期望过高而与焦虑作斗争。但梅西没有让焦虑削弱他的才华，因为他掌握了一种应对机制，这种机制同时也是他战术智慧背后的秘密。

在这最初的几分钟里，梅西做两件事。第一，他让自己冷静下来。第二，他观察对手。

一场足球比赛持续90分钟（外加几分钟“伤停补时”），大多数球员从第一分钟就积极参与比赛。哨声一响，他们就恳求队友传球，并执行教练赛前布置的战术。

但梅西以在开场几分钟不参与比赛而闻名。这是他的渐进式微调，随着他在越来越高的水平上踢球而逐渐发展起来。在开场几分钟里，梅西在中场附近来回踱步，几乎不与队友互动。其他球员在奔跑，有时甚至冲刺，而梅西大部分时间都在走路，很少超过慢跑的节奏。

在这最初的几分钟里，梅西做两件事。第一，他让自己冷静下来。轻松进入比赛是梅

ssi确保自己在比赛剩余时间内全神贯注的方式。他在场上呕吐的问题已经自行解决，部分原因或许是他找到了更有效的平复神经的方法。其次，他利用这段时间观察对手。他的双腿移动缓慢，但双眼在球员间迅速扫视，评估对手的优势、劣势和战术，同时监视己方球队在持球和无球时的跑动。梅西在比赛初期对球队的价值较低，但这种战术性的停顿提升了他在比赛剩余95%时间里的价值。

如果你将足球比赛分为“准备”和“投入”两个部分，梅西则高度依赖准备。在2017年梅西所在的巴塞罗那对阵宿敌皇家马德里的一场经典比赛中，梅西在90分钟的比赛里只跑了4分钟，走了80多分钟。然而，当他投入时，他充满活力，创造了9次机会，打入1球，并助攻队友再入1球。

正如你可能想象的那样，停顿比听起来更难。面对沉默和焦虑，我们的本能是行动。

这种模式对梅西来说并不罕见，而且往往在最重要的比赛中，他会强化自己的赛前准备。这种准备也解释了他为何能一次又一次地在正确的时间出现在正确的位置。尽管他的选位看起来超凡脱俗，但这并非奇迹；而是他每分钟都在学习，比如某个特定的后卫会漏掉球场上的某个特定区域，或者两名中场球员在向中场靠拢时会留出球场的一小片空当。

对我们其他人的启示很明确：当你感到焦虑时，无论是在体育竞技中还是更广泛的生活中，停顿一下。放慢脚步。做好准备。

正如你可能想象的那样，停顿比听起来更难。面对沉默和焦虑，我们的本能是行动。贾德森·布鲁尔，一位精神病学家和神经科学家，职业生涯中很大一部分时间都在思考如何“什么都不做”。

大约十五年前，布鲁尔开发了一种基于正念的成瘾治疗方法。

他的方法指导成瘾者在渴望时刻抵抗焦虑的浪潮，遵循一个首字母缩写为RAIN的四步法：

R——识别正在涌现的感受。

A——允许它存在。

I——探究你的情绪和想法（例如，“我现在身体里发生了什么？”）

N——逐刻留意正在发生的事情。

布鲁尔曾表示，他的方法受到临床心理学家塔拉·布拉赫的启发。为测试该方法，布鲁尔与努力戒烟的吸烟者合作。尼古丁成瘾以顽固著称——比许多能产生更强即时反应的硬性毒品更难戒除。

在推出该项目之前，

在布儒尔看来，他想在自己身上测试这套系统。问题是，“我本来不抽烟，”布儒尔写道，“但我需要能够理解那些觉得不抽烟脑袋就要爆炸的患者。”

尼古丁的半衰期大约为两小时，因此刚开始，吸烟者需要每次抵抗两小时的吸烟冲动。布儒尔推断，能够坚持两小时不吸烟的吸烟者会培养出新的不吸烟习惯，逐渐延长这些时段，直到他们完全不再感到吸烟的冲动。

他通过练习冥想两小时不动来模拟这些抵抗期。在坐立不安的时刻，他遵循RAIN步骤——识别、允许、探究、注意——如果他动了身体，计时器就会重置，他必须重新开始。

这听起来可能容易，但两小时静坐不动且没有娱乐活动是很长的时间。“令人惊讶的是，长时间不动并没有让我身体疼痛，”布儒尔写道，“而是坐立不安……那些渴望在喊‘起来！’”

几个月后，当大多数接受其他治疗方案的病人复发时，他的正念小组保持干净。

好几个月里，布儒尔都会接近成功，然后坐立不安击败了他。“然后有一天，”他写道，“我做到了。我坐满了整整两小时……之后每次静坐都越来越容易，因为我有信心能做到。而且我知道我的病人能戒烟。他们只需要合适的工具。”

布儒尔是对的。他的病人曾陷入困境，无法戒掉地球上最令人上瘾的物质之一。但当他进行一项又一项研究，将他的RAIN正念方法与当时最有效的成瘾治疗方法对比时，他的方法效果是那些方法的两倍多。

几个月后，当大多数接受其他治疗方案的病人复发时，他的正念小组保持干净。他们戒掉成瘾的可能性是其他人的五倍多，而这种方法本质上教他们在身体最迫切驱使他们行动的时刻暂停。

在布儒尔RAIN方法的四个步骤中，第二步——允许——或许是最关键的。允许一种体验冲刷你听起来简直太容易了，因为它不需要你做任何事情。但这正是关键点。它很难，因为尽管有行动的冲动，你却被迫什么都不做。

尽管暂停和准备有诸多好处，但有时主要事件不会按计划进行。梅西输过无数场比赛，而布儒尔的尼古丁成瘾者并非都在实验结束后的几周或几个月内保持戒断。掌握这些失败后的焦虑和不适至关重要，这是主要挑战之一。

取得突破的人与深陷困境无法自拔的人之间的关键差异。

readings.title: Why “Lake America” isn’t funny
body: Politics / Donald Trump / The Logoff Why “Lake America” isn’t funny ﻿Trump’s lake stunt, briefly explained. by Cameron Peters Aug 27, 2026, 10:20 PM UTC Gift Donald Trump displays a map labeling Lake Ontario as “Lake America” in the Oval Office of the White House on August 27, 2026. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here . Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump says he’s renaming Lake Ontario. Let’s talk about it. Can he really do that? Probably, though it doesn’t mean anyone will listen. Strictly speaking, Trump’s executive order, signed Thursday in the Oval Office, directs the Interior Department to update the lake’s name to “Lake America” in the US’s Geographic Names Information System. It remains to be seen whether products like Apple and Google maps will follow suit, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, whose state contains the US portion of the lake, says she won’t . Why is he doing that? The immediate answer is that Trump launched a trade war with Canada over the weekend, and he’s mad that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney won’t give him what he wants; this is a petty way to lash out. That doesn’t explain the trade war itself, though. Unfortunately, when my colleague, noted Canadian resident Zack Beauchamp, went looking earlier this week, he couldn’t find an explanation either. As he writes , there’s absolutely no constituency for this fight — other than Trump’s own imperial desires as he keeps joking-but-maybe-not-joking about making Canada the 51st state. The view from a very angry Canada Isn’t this just a stupid stunt? It’s a stupid stunt — but not just that. As my colleague Caitlin Dewey wrote earlier this week and Zack can attest, Canadians are royally pissed at the US. The trade war might feel like one more Trump fit of pique to Americans, but for Canadians, it’s a serious threat. Thursday’s executive order further ratchets up those tensions, and it specifically plays into the (very credible) school of thought that Trump isn’t really in this to redress US-Canada trade imbalances; as with many things Trump, it’s about dominance and the desire to claim a “win” at any cost. Lastly, it’s worth dwelling for a second on the stunt itself. One, Lake Ontario isn’t Canada’s name for it; it predates either country. And two, ad hoc renaming of bodies of water — this isn’t even the first time this Trump term — puts Trump in some fairly uncomfortable company . It’s all about dreaming big to build a better America, one with widespread high-speed rail, affordable housing, and infrastructure that works. ##段落
政治 / 唐纳德·特朗普 / 《The Logoff》 为什么“美洲湖”并不好笑 特朗普的湖泊噱头，简要解释。作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯 2026年8月27日，晚上10:20 UTC 赠送 唐纳德·特朗普于2026年8月27日在白宫椭圆形办公室展示一张将安大略湖标注为“美洲湖”的地图。安德鲁·哈尼克/盖蒂图片社 卡梅伦·彼得斯是Vox的编辑。本文首发于《The Logoff》，这是一份每日通讯，帮助你了解特朗普政府动态，同时不让政治新闻占据你的生活。在此订阅。

##段落
欢迎来到《The Logoff》：唐纳德·特朗普说他要把安大略湖改名。让我们来聊聊这件事。他真的能这么做吗？可能可以，但这不意味着会有人听。严格来说，特朗普周四在椭圆形办公室签署的行政命令，指示内政部在美国地理名称信息系统中将该湖的名称更新为“美洲湖”。苹果和谷歌地图等产品是否会跟进还有待观察，但纽约州州长凯西·霍楚尔——该州拥有该湖的美国部分——表示她不会配合。他为什么要这么做？直接的回答是，特朗普在周末对加拿大发动了贸易战，而他恼火于加拿大总理马克·卡尼不给他想要的东西；这是一种小气的发泄方式。但这并不能解释贸易战本身。不幸的是，当我的同事、知名加拿大居民扎克·博尚本周早些时候去寻找答案时，他也找不到解释。正如他所写的，这场斗争完全没有支持者——除了特朗普自己不断开玩笑但可能并非玩笑的、想让加拿大成为第51个州的帝国野心。

##段落
从一个非常愤怒的加拿大的视角来看 这不只是一个愚蠢的噱头吗？这是一个愚蠢的噱头——但不仅仅是。正如我的同事凯特琳·杜威本周早些时候所写、扎克也能证实的，加拿大人对美国极为愤怒。贸易战在美国人看来可能只是特朗普又一次意气用事，但对加拿大人来说，这是一个严重的威胁。周四的行政命令进一步加剧了这些紧张局势，并且特别印证了一种（非常可信的）观点，即特朗普的真正目的并非纠正美加贸易失衡；正如特朗普的许多事情一样，这关乎霸权和不惜一切代价“取胜”的欲望。最后，值得花点时间审视一下这个噱头本身。第一，安大略湖并不是加拿大起的名字；它比这两个国家的历史都更悠久。第二，随意给水域改名——这甚至不是特朗普本届任期内第一次这么做了——让特朗普置身于一些相当令人不安的同侪之列。

readings.title: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
body: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> Maria Petrishina / iStock

While there are various approaches to leading a team, many of us land on common questions in the search for an effective leadership style: How can I be there for my team? Do I need to command respect, or earn it? And the most crucial question of all: How can I make sure that my team trusts me?

Cady Coleman has been confronting these questions throughout her career as a chemist, engineer, Air Force colonel and astronaut. In conversation with TED science curator David Biello, Coleman shared three strategies to establish — and maintain — trust in a leader. Whatever your career is, these tips can help you to prepare your team to face any challenge you come across — in outer space or here on Earth.
People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team” … But maybe there should be.
1. Be brave enough to get to know your team members as individuals

People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team”… But maybe there should be, says Coleman. Every member of your team is a whole person, and since so many of the problems we face at work are interdisciplinary, understanding who each individual is beyond the 9-to-5 is valuable. Being vulnerable enough to get to know your team this way is an essential skill for any leader.

When you are able to say, “I think your world is different from mine, and I’d like to understand more about it,” you’re not just building trust; you’re opening a communication channel that teaches you more about your teammate’s qualities, says Coleman. This type of conversation requires the willingness and bravery to be vulnerable. Once you know what everyone brings to the table, you can foster the growth of qualities that can lead the team to collective success.

For example, as Coleman prepared for life on the space station, her advisors warned that the long periods of time away from family might be too much to handle. For her, however, this wasn’t a problem — she had been commuting and working away from her family for more than a decade. After sharing her experience, her colleagues realized she’d not only be adaptable to life on the space station, but also she could help others cope with the change, too.
2. Create a culture that’s open to everyone’s ideas
While leaders have to guide their teams, it’s equally important to let everyone know that they can advocate for themselves and bring their own ideas to the table.

Coleman benefitted from such leadership at NASA when she was training to go to the space station. In the face of budget cuts, NASA announced that they’d be eliminating their smaller space suits, meaning that if someone wasn’t qualified to use a larger space suit, they couldn’t go to the space station. This presented a choice for Coleman: wait for NASA to acquire suits that fit her or figure out how she could train in the larger suits. By working with NASA’s decision makers, Coleman was able to shift her training to use the bigger suits. Had she not felt the freedom to speak up, she says, she would have been waiting 10 years to go to the space station in a small suit.
When you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily.

Sometimes establishing trust in the workplace can be more difficult than you expect, but when you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily. Workplace dynamics are always changing — maybe a teammate’s work/life priorities have shifted, or a big mistake requires you all to work together under new pressures. These challenges make fostering trust tricky, but they are also moments of opportunity.

If a new challenge has arisen or trust has been breached, Coleman reminds us to “always figure out the why and the what.” Make sure to ask: why has this happened, why do they feel this way, and what can be done about it? Be open to different points of view, and don’t give up if you don’t get through at first. Connection is often in the smaller things you do; talk about food or music, write a note to compliment an idea and ask to hear more. This level of connection and vulnerability may not seem intuitive at first, but as you make trust a core part of your mission, it becomes easy.

Trust, Coleman reminds us, is both given and earned. As a woman, she knew gaining the trust of some male colleagues might be extra challenging. Her approach was simple: she performed well and, with patience and persistence, learned her colleagues’ language and taught them hers. The challenges in gaining trust will always be there, but if you model vulnerability, openness and understanding for your team, you’ll find the rewards will always be there, too.

This post was adapted from a recent LinkedIn Live conversation with Cady Coleman, former NASA Astronaut and author of the forthcoming book, Sharing Space: An Astronaut’s Guide to Mission, Wonder, and Making Change , due out July 2024.

有效领导的3个策略，来自一位前宇航员
2023年12月4日
/
约瑟夫·德布林
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
Reddit
WhatsApp
玛丽亚·彼得里希娜 / iStock
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> 玛丽亚·彼得里希娜 / iStock
领导力是什么样的？

虽然带领团队的方法多种多样，但许多人在寻找有效领导风格时，都会遇到一些共同的问题：我该如何支持我的团队？我需要命令别人尊重，还是赢得尊重？而最关键的问题是：我怎样才能确保团队信任我？

凯迪·科尔曼在作为化学家、工程师、空军上校和宇航员的职业生涯中，一直在面对这些问题。在与TED科学策展人大卫·比埃洛的对话中，科尔曼分享了建立并维持领导者信任的三种策略。无论你的职业是什么，这些建议都能帮助你让团队准备好迎接你遇到的任何挑战——无论是在外太空还是在地球上。

人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但也许应该有。

1. 勇敢地去了解你的团队成员，把他们当作独立的个体

人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但也许应该有，科尔曼说。你团队中的每个成员都是一个完整的人，而由于我们在工作中遇到的许多问题都是跨学科的，了解每个人在朝九晚五之外是什么样的，是非常有价值的。以足够的坦诚，用这种方式去了解你的团队，是任何领导者必备的技能。

科尔曼说，当你能说出“我觉得你的世界和我的不同，我想更多地了解它”时，你不仅仅是在建立信任；你是在打开一条沟通渠道，让你更了解队友的特质。这种对话需要愿意和勇气去展现脆弱。一旦你知道每个人能带来什么，你就能培养那些能带领团队走向集体成功的特质。

例如，当科尔曼为空间站生活做准备时，她的顾问警告说，长时间离开家人可能难以承受。然而，对她来说，这不是问题——她已经通勤并远离家人工作十多年了。在分享了自己的经历后，她的同事意识到，她不仅能适应空间站的生活，还能帮助其他人应对这种变化。

2. 创造一种对每个人的想法都开放的文化

虽然领导者必须引导团队，但同样重要的是，让每个人都知道他们可以为自己发声，并把自己的想法带到台面上来。

科尔曼在NASA训练时，就受益于这样的领导力，当时她正在为前往太空做准备。

面对预算削减，美国国家航空航天局宣布将淘汰较小号的太空服，这意味着如果某人不符合使用较大号太空服的资格，就无法前往空间站。这对科尔曼来说是一个选择：等待NASA获得适合她的太空服，或者想办法训练自己使用较大的太空服。通过与NASA的决策者合作，科尔曼得以调整训练，使用较大的太空服。她说，如果她没有感到可以自由发声，她可能会等上十年才能穿着小号太空服前往空间站。  
当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其他事情就会更容易水到渠成。  
##段落
3. 让信任成为你的使命  
有时在工作场所建立信任可能比你预期的更困难，但当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其他事情就会更容易水到渠成。职场动态总是在变化——也许队友的工作/生活优先级发生了转变，或者一个大错误要求你们在新压力下共同合作。这些挑战使培养信任变得棘手，但它们也是机遇的时刻。  
如果出现了新的挑战或信任被破坏，科尔曼提醒我们要“始终弄清楚原因和内容”。务必询问：为什么会发生这种情况，他们为什么会有这样的感受，以及可以对此做些什么？对不同观点保持开放态度，如果一开始没有突破，不要放弃。联系往往体现在你做的那些小事中：谈论食物或音乐，写一张便条赞美一个想法并请求了解更多。这种联系和脆弱的程度起初可能看起来不太直观，但当你把信任作为使命的核心部分时，它就会变得容易。  
科尔曼提醒我们，信任既是给予的，也是赢得的。作为一名女性，她知道赢得一些男性同事的信任可能格外具有挑战性。她的方法很简单：她表现出色，并以耐心和坚持，学会了同事们的语言，也教会了他们她的语言。建立信任的挑战将永远存在，但如果你为团队树立脆弱、开放和理解的榜样，你会发现回报也永远存在。  
这篇文章改编自最近一次与凯迪·科尔曼的LinkedIn Live对话，她是前NASA宇航员，即将出版的新书《共享空间：宇航员的任务、奇迹与变革指南》将于2024年7月发行。  
在这里观看完整的LinkedIn对话：  
来自我们合作伙伴美国空军的消息：美国空军的使命是飞行、战斗并获胜——随时随地提供空中力量。无论是全职、兼职、穿制服还是不穿制服，每个服役人员都在帮助我们实现任务成功中扮演着关键角色。

readings.title: The best mangrove photography of 2026
body: 15 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Harrison Jones Eerie trees, prowling tigers and rare dolphin hunting behaviours have been featured at the 2026 Mangrove Photography Awards. Found where tropical plants meet saltwater, mangrove forests hang in the balance between land and sea. These eerie ecosystems are home to some of the world's most fascinating wildlife. For some rare species, mangroves provide respite and protection. For others, they are a hunting ground – including this this juvenile royal Bengal tiger in India (pictured above), in the world's largest mangrove forest, the Sundarbans. These images from the 2026 Mangrove Photography Awards capture the extraordinary beauty and fragility of the world's mangrove forests. Here you can explore 13 of the competition's most striking entries, from Florida to Indonesia. The overall winner of the competition was this eye-catching picture of a hidden "ghost net", glowing under ultraviolet light. The image, shot by Gaurav Patil, shows the net tangled in a mangrove on a tide-swept shore south of Mumbai, India. Discarded fishing nets become a hazard to wildlife when trapped in mangroves. Also pictured in the Indian Sundarbans are these two colourful mudskippers, who walk, jump and breathe on land – skirting the transition zone between land and sea, much like mangroves do.  Mangrove trees are found along coasts and estuaries of more than 100 countries in the tropics and subtropics. In the Bahamas, this rare reddish egret stands out among the greenery. The bottlenose dolphins of Florida Bay, US, are resourceful animals. The mangrove-lined coast provides them with their prey, including mullet. They trap the fish in a ring of mud they stir up from below, using the silty water like a net. This hunting strategy is almost unique to the dolphins of Florida Bay, and rarely captured on camera. Mangroves provide a complex underwater habitat, as this shot of a young green turtle swimming among a web of roots shows. When water levels rise with the tide, this area becomes a flourishing ecosystem and offers shelter from predators, including tiger sharks. Another shot from Florida Bay took the top prize in the birds category. It features American flamingos closely observing a lemon shark. Just off the Galapagos Islands, a group of golden rays were pictured drifting past a shallow mangrove cove. Mangroves not only support biodiversity themselves, but also help adjacent ecosystems, such as nearby seagrass meadows or coral reefs .   Mangrove forests are associated with more than 1,500 species , and provide nursery habitats for many commercially important fish. This shot shows a school of baitfish sheltering in Lac Bay, Bonaire, as a snook darts towards them.  Mangroves can store as much as five times more carbon than land-based forests. Roots slow incoming waves and protect communities from storm surges – while branches also offer refuge to birds, like this charming Indian white-eye, landing on a mangrove tree in Iran. Kallol Mukherjee's picture won the mammals category and shows dense vegetation offering protection to jungle cat kittens. By one estimate , mangroves also offer coastal protection for more than 150 million people by stabilising shorelines and reducing erosion. Mangroves also sequester significant quantities of CO2. The competition's "on the ground" winner, shot by Ryuhei Suguri, shows a solitary mangrove tree in Indonesia, illuminated under the Milky Way. Mangrove forests face numerous threats from humans, including pollution – as this image highlights in grim detail. Deforestation is another major risk, with many mangroves at risk of clearing for fish farming, agriculture or coastal development, as well as the impacts of climate change.  More like this: • The Caribbean mangrove forest that defied destruction • How mangrove forests helped stall environmental crime • Why worm poaching is threatening India's wetlands Yet there are reasons to be hopeful: according to Global Mangrove Watch , the extent of mangrove cover worldwide has seen a net increase of 477.2 sq km (180 sq miles) between 1985 and 2025. 诡异的树木、潜行的老虎和罕见的海豚捕猎行为，亮相2026年红树林摄影奖。红树林生长在热带植物与海水交汇之处，悬于陆地与海洋之间。这些诡异的生态系统是世界上最迷人的野生动物的家园。对一些珍稀物种而言，红树林提供栖息之所与庇护；对另一些物种来说，它们则是狩猎场——包括上图这只在印度孙德尔本斯（世界最大红树林）中的幼年孟加拉虎。  
这些来自2026年红树林摄影奖的作品，捕捉了世界红树林非凡的美丽与脆弱。从佛罗里达到印度尼西亚，你可以在这里欣赏到比赛中13幅最引人注目的作品。  
该比赛的总冠军是这幅引人注目的照片，展示了一张隐藏的“幽灵渔网”在紫外线下发出光芒。这张由Gaurav Patil拍摄的图像，显示渔网缠绕在印度孟买南部一处潮汐冲刷海岸的红树林中。废弃的渔网一旦困在红树林中，便成为野生动物的隐患。  
同样拍摄于印度孙德尔本斯的，还有这两只色彩斑斓的弹涂鱼，它们在陆地上行走、跳跃和呼吸——穿梭于陆地与海洋的过渡地带，正如红树林本身。  
红树林分布在热带和亚热带100多个国家的海岸和河口。在巴哈马，这只罕见的红鹭在绿意中格外醒目。  
美国佛罗里达湾的宽吻海豚是足智多谋的动物。红树林覆盖的海岸为它们提供猎物，包括鲻鱼。它们用从下方搅起的泥圈困住鱼群，利用浑浊的水体如同一张网。这种捕猎策略几乎为佛罗里达湾的海豚所独有，且极少被镜头捕捉到。  
红树林提供复杂的海底栖息环境，正如这张照片所示：一只幼年绿海龟在盘根错节的根系间游动。当潮水上涨、水位升高时，这片区域成为繁茂的生态系统，并为躲避虎鲨等捕食者提供庇护。  
另一张来自佛罗里达湾的照片赢得了鸟类类别的最高奖。画面中，美洲火烈鸟正密切观察一条柠檬鲨。  
就在加拉帕戈斯群岛附近，一群金色鳐鱼被拍到漂过一片浅水红树林湾。红树林不仅自身支持生物多样性，还帮助邻近生态系统，如附近的海草床或珊瑚礁。  
红树林与1500多个物种相关联，并为许多具有商业价值的重要鱼类提供育苗栖息地。这张照片显示一群饵鱼在博内尔岛拉克湾避难，而一条梭鱼正冲向它们。  
红树林的碳储存量可达同等面积热带森林的五倍之多。

陆地上的森林。树根能减缓海浪的冲击，保护社区免受风暴潮的侵袭——而树枝也为鸟类提供了栖息之所，比如这只迷人的印度白眼鸟，正落在伊朗的一棵红树林树上。卡洛尔·慕克吉的照片赢得了哺乳动物类奖项，画面展示了茂密的植被为丛林猫幼崽提供庇护。据估计，红树林还能通过稳定海岸线和减少侵蚀，为超过1.5亿人提供沿海保护。红树林还能封存大量的二氧化碳。本次比赛“实地”类获奖作品由龙谷修平拍摄，展示了印度尼西亚一棵孤独的红树林树，在银河系的照耀下熠熠生辉。红树林面临来自人类的众多威胁，包括污染——这张图片以令人不安的细节凸显了这一点。森林砍伐是另一个主要风险，许多红树林面临被清伐的风险，用于水产养殖、农业或沿海开发，同时还受到气候变化的影响。更多相关内容：• 加勒比海红树林森林如何抵御破坏• 红树林森林如何帮助阻止环境犯罪• 为什么蠕虫偷猎正威胁印度的湿地然而，仍有理由保持希望：据全球红树林观察组织称，1985年至2025年间，全球红树林覆盖面积净增加了477.2平方公里（180平方英里）。你可以在这里查看更多2026年红树林摄影奖的获奖作品。——如需将重要的气候新闻和充满希望的发展动态发送至您的收件箱，请订阅《未来地球》通讯，而《要点清单》每周两次为您提供精心挑选的特写和洞察。欲了解更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境和健康报道，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。地球自然与户外野生动物动物森林海洋气候变化环境特写

readings.title: Why are more Americans moving to Ireland?
body: 15 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Anne Cassidy In a historic reversal, the number of Americans moving to Ireland last year was higher than the number of Irish people migrating to the US. Was this just a blip or the start of a more profound trend? Michael Sable is an American stand-up comedian and communications manager who moved from Washington DC to Dublin in 2016.  Sable, who draws on his experience of being an American living in the Republic of Ireland in his stand-up routine, says that, when he first arrived, many Irish people he met were surprised he'd made the move, but now they don't question it.  "I've noticed that, as the years go on, people have been less and less incredulous when hearing that an American moved to Ireland," he says.  Sable is one of a rising number of people who have moved to Ireland from the US, with the latest data showing the figure nearly doubling from  4,900 to 9,600 between 2024 and 2025 ,  exceeding the number of Irish people headed in the opposite direction.   It comes as the US saw more people leave than arrive last year, according to a report from US think tank the  Brookings Institution . It said this was the first time that this had been the case "in at least half a century".  The think tank highlighted "dramatic changes in immigration policy" under the second administration of President Trump, including more removals of undocumented foreign workers, and the White House "all but suspend[ing]" the US programme for accepting refugees.    Separately, more American citizens are choosing to move abroad than ever before, says the  Wall Street Journal.  It calculated that "at least 180,000 Americans" voluntarily left the US in 2025, which it said was a record high.   The reversal in the flow of migration between Ireland and the US marks a historic turning point in the shared history of the two countries, which have deep-rooted ties.  For centuries, millions of Irish people emigrated to the US in search of work or a better life, making Irish Americans one of the country's largest ethnic groups. There have been several US presidents with Irish ancestry, including John F Kennedy and Joe Biden, whose visits to Ireland were  celebrated more like homecomings  than diplomatic missions.   Irish writer Colm Tóibín has frequently explored the relationship between Ireland and the US in his work, particularly in his novels, Brooklyn and Long Island, which follow the story of an Irish girl who emigrates to America in the 1950s.  Tóibín, who lives in the US, says the relationship between the US and Ireland has changed. "A myth was created that America was a great place of opportunity and wealth," he says. "It was built into the [Irish] culture that if there's any trouble, you go to England, if there's any ambition or spark you go to America." "The flow of young people [from Ireland to the US] looking for work just hasn't continued. So, that is going to be a big change in the future, because you're not going to get the same easy connection between Ireland and America," he adds.  The trend partly reflects political shifts in both countries. As well as developing into a high-tech, export-driven knowledge economy, Ireland has undergone a social transformation in recent decades, moving from a deeply conservative society to a liberal, progressive nation, following referendums on divorce, abortion and gay marriage.    Tóibín, who was a prominent campaigner for the "yes" vote in Ireland’s same-sex marriage referendum, says: "Everyone became more aware that Ireland was a more liberal, cosmopolitan, open society, and that it would be a good place to live." By contrast, the US has moved to the political right under President Trump, who, since returning to office, has launched a major crackdown on illegal immigration.   Tóibín revisits the Irish-American immigrant experience in his latest short story collection, The News from Dublin. In one story in the collection, Five Bridges, the protagonist is an undocumented Irish immigrant preparing to leave America before US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as Ice, come looking for him. The number of Irish citizens deported from the US  rose by more than 50%  in 2025.  "There are large numbers of Irish people in America who are official in every way – they pay taxes, own their own house, have kids in school, but they came in on a tourist visa," says Tóibín. "If Ice found them, Ice would detain them. That's really frightening." Expatsi, a firm that helps US citizens to move abroad,  reported it experienced a month's worth of traffic  in the hours after President Trump's election in 2024. Expatsi co-founder Jen Barnett says the reasons Americans cite for leaving are wide-ranging. "[Factors include] what's going on politically in the US, and has been for 10 years, the cost of living, and then safety. Gun violence is so prevalent," she says.  Politics was also a driving factor for Kevin Wozniak, an American lecturer living in Ireland. He and his husband left Boston in 2023 after he got a post at Maynooth University, 23km (14 miles) west of Dublin.  "My motivation to look at opportunities abroad was deep fears about the trajectory of the country in the era of Donald Trump," Wozniak says. "Ireland has liberalised very significantly and has moved in exactly the opposite direction that the US is moving." Natalia Lange, a migrant support worker based in Crosshaven, county Cork, moved there from Michigan with her husband after the 2024 US election. Lange, who is half-Hungarian and has an EU passport, dreamed of living in Ireland since visiting on a school trip. "Politically, Ireland aligns much more with how we think," she says. "The US has the infrastructure to take in a lot more people, but it's a lot less inviting." Lauren Udoh, from Houston, Texas, moved to Claregalway, in county Galway, in 2021 after marrying her Irish husband. Udoh, who has two young children, works as an executive assistant and documents expat life on social media under the moniker TheGalwayGal.  "One of the biggest benefits is safety. I feel a lot safer here," she says. "With kids going to school, you don’t have to worry about school shootings." Emigration from Ireland has fallen, with 65,600 people leaving in the year to April 2025, a  6% decrease on 2024 , according to the Irish Central Statistics Office (CSO). For those wanting to live abroad, Australia is the most popular destination.  The CSO said 13,500 people left Ireland for Australia in the year to April 2025, the highest level since 2013. This is more than double the estimated 6,100 people who left Ireland for the US, which was, however, still up 22% on the previous year.   Restrictions around J1 visas, which allow Irish university students to work and travel in the US, has caused many  Irish students to rethink studying in the US.    Karen McHugh, CEO at Safe Home Ireland, an organisation supporting Irish-born emigrants wishing to return to Ireland, says: "We've certainly noticed an increase in queries about returning [from the US to Ireland]," she says. "Australia and Canada are two major countries where people are now going to from Ireland, and that's ease of getting a visa." Irish student Jamie McElhinney is currently on a work placement in Portugal as part of his hospitality management course. McElhinney, who studies at Dundalk Institute of Technology, says current immigration controls put him off seeking a work placement in the US. "I was going to go to Boston, and then all of the news about Ice started coming out. It’s a deterrent from going over there," he says.  While there are opportunities in Ireland, with  employment at 74.4%,  there is also a growing housing crisis, with recent  protests  over the shortage of affordable housing.  Barnett says the housing shortage is something the Americans her company helps to relocate are mindful of, adding: "They don't want to add to [the housing crisis], so one of the things we talk to them about is staying out of city centres." Sable, whose Irish grandparents emigrated to the US in 1939, is one of many Americans whose ancestry enabled them to get an Irish passport. Applications for Irish passports in the US rose by 10% in 2024 , the Irish Department of Foreign Affairs reported.  Sable now thinks of Ireland as home. "Culturally, I identify a lot more with Irish people," he says. "It's a very collective society, not huge on individualism like in the US." More like this:  •  Why Ireland's film industry is booming    •  Is New York's cannabis business flying high?   •  The 'brutal' toll of war on Dubai’s tourist trade Bill Hillyard, another American with Irish roots, relocated to Ireland for the cooler climate. He and his wife Anne left California following wildfires in 2019. "My wife said we need to move somewhere where it rains." They now run a pub called The Algiers in Baltimore, Co Cork.  Hillyard says he now tries to avoid turbulent events in the US. "I tried not to follow the news because I'm here now," he says. "But I'm reminded every day, because everyone asks me about Trump and what's going on there… I'm West Cork's ambassador to the US at this point." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. 2026年4月15日 分享 保存 设为谷歌偏好 安妮·卡西迪 在一场历史性的逆转中，去年移居爱尔兰的美国人数量超过了移居美国的爱尔兰人数量。这只是一次偶然波动，还是更深层趋势的开端？迈克尔·萨布尔是一位美国单口喜剧演员兼传播经理，他于2016年从华盛顿特区搬到了都柏林。萨布尔在表演中融入了自己作为美国人在爱尔兰共和国生活的经历，他说，刚来时遇到的许多爱尔兰人都对他的搬迁感到惊讶，但现在他们不再质疑了。“我注意到，随着时间推移，人们听到有美国人搬到爱尔兰时，越来越不觉得难以置信了，”他说。萨布尔是从美国移居爱尔兰的日益增多的人群中的一员，最新数据显示，这一数字在2024年至2025年间从4,900人几乎翻倍至9,600人，超过了反向流动的爱尔兰人数量。

##段落

与此同时，根据美国智库布鲁金斯学会的一份报告，去年美国离境人数超过了入境人数。该报告称，这是“至少半个世纪以来”首次出现这种情况。该智库强调了特朗普总统第二任期内“移民政策的剧烈变化”，包括更多驱逐无证外国工人，以及白宫“几乎全面暂停”了美国接收难民的计划。此外，《华尔街日报》称，选择移居海外的美国公民比以往任何时候都多。该报计算，2025年“至少有18万美国人”自愿离开美国，并称这是创纪录的高位。

##段落

爱尔兰与美国之间移民流向的逆转，标志着两国深厚渊源共同历史中的一个历史性转折点。几个世纪以来，数百万爱尔兰人移居美国寻找工作或更好的生活，使爱尔兰裔美国人成为该国最大的族群之一。多位美国总统拥有爱尔兰血统，包括约翰·F·肯尼迪和乔·拜登，他们对爱尔兰的访问更像是归乡而非外交使命。

##段落

爱尔兰作家科尔姆·托宾经常在作品中探讨爱尔兰与美国的关系，尤其是他的小说《布鲁克林》和《长岛》，这两部作品讲述了一个爱尔兰女孩在20世纪50年代移居美国的故事。居住在美国的托宾表示，美国与爱尔兰之间的关系已经改变。“曾有一个神话，说美国是充满机遇和财富的伟大之地，”他说。“这在爱尔兰文化中根深蒂固——如果遇到麻烦，就去英格兰；如果有抱负，

##段落
或者让你去美国。” “从爱尔兰到美国寻找工作的年轻人潮并没有持续下去。所以，这将是未来的一大变化，因为你不会再有爱尔兰和美国之间那种轻松的联系了，”他补充道。这一趋势部分反映了两国的政治转变。爱尔兰不仅发展成了高科技、出口导向的知识经济体，还在近几十年经历了社会转型，从深度保守的社会走向自由、进步的国家，这得益于关于离婚、堕胎和同性婚姻的公投。托宾曾是爱尔兰同性婚姻公投中“赞成”票的著名活动家，他说：“每个人都更加意识到，爱尔兰是一个更自由、更国际化、更开放的社会，而且会是一个宜居的好地方。”相比之下，美国在特朗普总统领导下转向了政治右翼，他重返白宫后对非法移民发起了大规模打击。托宾在他最新的短篇小说集《都柏林的消息》中重新审视了爱尔兰裔美国移民的经历。在该集的一个故事《五座桥》中，主人公是一名无证爱尔兰移民，正准备在美国移民和海关执法局（简称Ice）找上门之前离开美国。2025年，被美国驱逐出境的爱尔兰公民人数上升了超过50%。“在美国有大量爱尔兰人，他们在各方面都是合法的——他们纳税、拥有自己的房子、孩子在学校上学，但他们是以旅游签证入境的，”托宾说。“如果Ice找到他们，Ice会拘留他们。这真的很可怕。”帮助美国公民移居国外的公司Expatsi报告称，在2024年特朗普总统当选后的几个小时内，其网站流量就相当于一个月的量。Expatsi联合创始人詹·巴内特表示，美国人选择离开的原因多种多样。“（因素包括）美国国内的政治形势，而且已经持续了十年，生活成本，还有安全问题。枪支暴力太普遍了，”她说。政治也是居住爱尔兰的美国讲师凯文·沃兹尼亚克离开的驱动因素。他和丈夫于2023年离开波士顿，当时他在都柏林以西23公里（14英里）的梅努斯大学获得了一个职位。“我寻找海外机会的动力是对唐纳德·特朗普时代国家走向的深深恐惧，”沃兹尼亚克说。“爱尔兰已经非常显著地自由化，并且朝着与美国截然相反的方向发展。”娜塔莉亚·兰格是科克郡克罗斯黑文的移民支持工作者，她在2024年美国大选后与丈夫从密歇根搬到了那里。兰格有一半匈牙利血统，持有欧盟护照，她梦想着住在爱尔兰，啜

##段落

一次学校旅行时曾到访过爱尔兰。“在政治上，爱尔兰的思维方式与我们更为契合，”她说，“美国有基础设施接纳更多人，但那里显得不那么友好。”来自得克萨斯州休斯顿的劳伦·乌多于2021年嫁给爱尔兰丈夫后，搬到戈尔韦郡的克莱尔加尔韦。乌多有两个年幼的孩子，担任行政助理，并以“TheGalwayGal”的名义在社交媒体上记录外籍生活。“最大的好处之一是安全。我觉得这里安全得多，”她说，“孩子上学时，你不用担心校园枪击事件。”据爱尔兰中央统计局数据，爱尔兰的移民出境人数已下降，截至2025年4月的一年中有65,600人离开，比2024年减少6%。对于想移居海外的人来说，澳大利亚是最受欢迎的目的地。中央统计局称，截至2025年4月的一年中，有13,500人从爱尔兰前往澳大利亚，为2013年以来的最高水平。这一数字是前往美国（估计6,100人）的两倍多，但赴美人数仍比前一年增长了22%。J1签证允许爱尔兰大学生在美国工作和旅行，而相关限制已使许多爱尔兰学生重新考虑赴美留学。

支持希望返回爱尔兰的爱尔兰裔移民组织Safe Home Ireland的首席执行官凯伦·麦克休说：“我们确实注意到，关于（从美国）返回爱尔兰的咨询有所增加。”她说：“澳大利亚和加拿大是爱尔兰人现在前往的两个主要国家，这得益于签证获取的便利性。”爱尔兰学生杰米·麦克尔欣尼目前作为酒店管理课程的一部分在葡萄牙实习。就读于邓多克理工学院的麦克尔欣尼表示，当前的移民管制让他打消了去美国实习的念头。“我本来要去波士顿，然后关于移民执法局的各种新闻就开始涌现。这让人不敢去那边，”他说。虽然爱尔兰存在就业机会，就业率达74.4%，但住房危机也在加剧，近期出现了关于经济适用房短缺的抗议活动。巴内特说，住房短缺是她公司帮助迁移的美国人所关注的问题，并补充道：“他们不想加剧（住房危机），所以我们与他们讨论的要点之一就是避开市中心。”塞布尔的祖父母于1939年从爱尔兰移民到美国，他是众多凭借血统获得爱尔兰护照的美国人之一。爱尔兰外交部报告称，2024年美国申请爱尔兰护照的人数增长了10%。塞布尔现在把爱尔兰视为家。“在文化上，我与爱尔兰人的认同感要强得多，”他说，“这是一个非常……

集体社会，不像美国那样强调个人主义。"更多类似内容：
• 为什么爱尔兰电影业蓬勃发展
• 纽约的大麻生意是否蒸蒸日上
• 战争对迪拜旅游业的“残酷”打击

另一位有爱尔兰血统的美国人比尔·希利亚德为了更凉爽的气候移居爱尔兰。他和妻子安妮在2019年加州野火后离开了那里。“我妻子说我们需要搬到一个下雨的地方。”他们现在在科克郡巴尔的摩经营一家名为阿尔及尔斯的酒吧。希利亚德说，他现在尽量避免关注美国的动荡事件。“我尽量不关注新闻，因为我现在在这里，”他说，“但我每天都会被提醒，因为每个人都问我特朗普的事以及那边的情况……我现在是西科克驻美国的大使了。”

readings.title: What Dolly Parton taught us about how to give
body: Future Perfect What Dolly Parton taught us about how to give ﻿The late icon made being a good person look easy. by Sara Herschander Aug 26, 2026, 9:40 PM UTC Dolly Parton proved that helping others is not only easy to do, but can be a lot of fun. Katherine Bomboy/NBC Sara Herschander is a reporter for Vox, focusing on infrastructure, and how America builds, or fails to build, the hidden systems shaping much of everyday life, from how we get our water to the cables that keep the lights on. Dolly Parton was on her way to the studio to polish off “ Blue Smoke ” when the SUV she was riding in collided with a sedan in a Nashville intersection in 2013. At the hospital, she struck an unlikely friendship with her physician, Naji Abumrad, who, like Parton, was raised in a misty mountain village, hers in East Tennessee and his in Lebanon. “It’s just like how you meet people in your life. You just click, you just feel like you know them,” Parton once told his son, Jad Abumrad, a public radio host who interviewed Parton for a nine-part series on her life. “There are just some things that, you know, you just can’t explain it. You just be it, you just live it, you just know it, and you just feel it.” The whole world, it seems, felt it — that inexplicably swift, sweet connection — with Dolly Parton herself, a light-filled, lifelong philanthropist in the truest, most etymological sense of the word: a lover of humankind. Some seven years after their friendship began, Abumrad told Parton that his fellow researchers at Vanderbilt University Medical Center were looking into a possible vaccine for Covid-19, which had just begun to rage across the country. Without missing a beat, Parton wrote a check for $1 million, an early contribution toward what would eventually become the Moderna vaccine against Covid-19. Her donation “made the research towards the vaccine go 10 times faster than it would be without it,” Abumrad later told the Washington Post , calling his friend “the kindest and most philanthropic human being” he’d ever known. Parton, who died at the age of 80 yesterday, was raised with her 11 siblings amid poverty in the Smoky Mountains of Eastern Tennessee. She often credited her upbringing as a muse for both her music and her generosity. Just as integral to her persona as her kitschy high-femme glamour, her poofy hair and rhinestones, was Parton’s capacity for helping others. With an infectious sense of joy and optimism, she proved that helping others is not only easy to do, but can be a lot of fun. Parton’s most famous foray into philanthropy by far was her Imagination Library, which she founded in 1995 in honor of her father, who never learned to read or write. Since then, the initiative has doled out a jaw-dropping over 300 million free children’s books to young kids around the country and the world. “I just give from my heart,” she remarked while accepting the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy, a kind of Nobel Prize for giving, in 2022. “I never know what I’m going to do or why I’m gonna do it. I just see a need, and if I can fill it, then I will.” After wildfires tore through her native Tennessee in 2016, she raised millions of dollars that she used to give thousands of dollars in direct cash payments to hundreds of families who’d lost their homes. In recent years, she’s given millions of dollars to families affected by Hurricane Helene, to pediatric infectious-disease research, and to children’s charities across Tennessee. Back in 1990, Parton helped open a sanctuary for injured eagles in partnership with conservationists at Dollywood, the Eagle Mountain Sanctuary, which was forced to close after a brutal storm earlier this year. (You can donate to the American Eagle Foundation, which is rehoming Dollyland’s eagles here .) Parton, who had a net worth of about $450 million according to Forbes , may have given away many other donations privately. In 2006, when asked about the full scope of her donations, she told my former colleagues at The Chronicle of Philanthropy with her characteristic sass that “it’s none of your business. I have often said that I count my blessings a whole lot more than I count my money,” she said, “the same is true for the contributions I make.” The world may have gotten a peek into her private giving a few years ago, when some savvy social media users helped break the news that Parton had been casually paying for band uniforms at high schools across Tennessee, and had been quietly doing so for decades. She also received $100 million as a recipient of Jeff Bezos’s Courage and Civility Award to give away as she saw fit. It’s unclear where she chose to spend that money, but it could certainly buy a lot of school band uniforms, children’s books, or pediatric hospital wings. There was always something otherworldly about Parton’s kindness. It was as if the nicest person you’ve ever met found herself in possession of hundreds of millions of dollars in cash. But as serious as her contributions were — to the music industry, and to millions of children around the country — she never took herself too seriously, and maybe that’s what made it feel so enthralling to watch. “I’m kind of addicted to the feeling of giving,” she told People in 2021, “knowing that I’m doing something good for someone else.” And that’s a lesson that all of us, legendary multimillionaire country superstar or not, can use to help carry her legacy forward. ##段落
未来完美：多莉·帕顿教给我们如何给予
这位已故偶像让做个好人看起来轻而易举。作者：萨拉·赫尚德，2026年8月26日，晚上9:40 UTC
多莉·帕顿证明了帮助他人不仅轻而易举，而且可以充满乐趣。凯瑟琳·邦博伊/NBC
萨拉·赫尚德是Vox的记者，专注于基础设施，以及美国如何建造——或未能建造——那些塑造日常生活大部分面貌的隐形系统，从我们如何获取水源到维持灯光长明的电缆。

##段落
2013年，多莉·帕顿在前往录音室打磨《Blue Smoke》的途中，她乘坐的SUV在纳什维尔一个十字路口与一辆轿车相撞。在医院里，她与医生纳吉·阿布穆拉德结下了一段意想不到的友谊——阿布穆拉德和帕顿一样，成长于一个云雾缭绕的山村，她来自田纳西州东部，而他来自黎巴嫩。“就像你生命中遇到人的方式一样。你们就是合拍，就是觉得好像认识他们，”帕顿曾这样告诉他的儿子贾德·阿布穆拉德，这位公共广播主持人曾为制作一档关于帕顿生平的九集系列节目而采访过她。“有些事情，你知道，就是无法解释。你就是成为它，活在其中，知道它，感受它。”

##段落
整个世界似乎都感受到了那种与多莉·帕顿本人之间无法言说却又迅速、甜蜜的联结——她是一位充满光芒、终身行善的慈善家，用这个词最纯粹、最词源学的意义来说：一个热爱人类的人。在他们友谊开始大约七年后，阿布穆拉德告诉帕顿，他在范德比尔特大学医学中心的同事们正在研究一种可能的新冠疫苗，而那时疫情刚刚开始席卷全美。帕顿毫不犹豫地开出了一张100万美元的支票，为最终成为莫德纳新冠疫苗的项目提供了早期资助。她的捐赠“让疫苗研究的进展比没有这笔资金时快了十倍”，阿布穆拉德后来告诉《华盛顿邮报》，并称他的朋友是“我认识的最善良、最具慈善心的人”。

##段落
帕顿于昨天去世，享年80岁。她与11个兄弟姐妹在田纳西州东部大烟山的贫困中长大。她常将自己的成长经历视为音乐和慷慨的灵感源泉。与她标志性的俗艳高女性化魅力、蓬松发型和水钻装饰一样，帕顿帮助他人的能力同样是其人格中不可或缺的一部分。带着一种富有感染力的喜悦与乐观，她证明了帮助他人不仅轻而易举，而且可以充满乐趣。

##段落
帕顿最著名的慈善事业当属她的“想象图书馆”，这是她于1995年为纪念从未学会读写父亲而创办的。自那以来，该计划已向孩子们免费发放了超过3亿册图书，数字令人瞠目结舌。

她激励着全国乃至全世界的孩子们。“我只是发自内心地给予，”她在2022年接受卡内基慈善奖章（相当于慈善界的诺贝尔奖）时说道，“我从来不知道自己会做什么，也不知道为什么去做。我只是看到需求，如果我能满足，我就会去做。”2016年，野火席卷她的家乡田纳西州后，她筹集了数百万美元，直接向数百个失去家园的家庭发放了数千美元的现金补助。近年来，她向受飓风海伦妮影响的家庭、儿科传染病研究以及田纳西州的儿童慈善机构捐赠了数百万美元。早在1990年，帕顿就与环保主义者合作，在多莉坞开设了一个受伤鹰类庇护所——鹰山庇护所，但该庇护所在今年早些时候的一场猛烈风暴后被迫关闭。（你可以向美国鹰基金会捐款，该基金会正在为多莉坞的鹰类重新安置家园。）据《福布斯》报道，帕顿的净资产约为4.5亿美元，她可能还私下进行了许多其他捐赠。2006年，当被问及她捐赠的全部范围时，她以特有的俏皮口吻告诉我《慈善纪事报》的前同事们：“这不关你的事。我经常说，我数 blessings 的次数远比数钱多，”她说，“我对自己的贡献也是如此。”几年前，世界可能得以一窥她的私人捐赠，当时一些精明的社交媒体用户帮助爆料，帕顿一直在为田纳西州各地高中的乐队制服买单，而且已经默默做了几十年。她还作为杰夫·贝索斯“勇气与文明奖”的获得者收到了1亿美元，可按她的意愿支配。目前尚不清楚她选择将这些钱花在哪里，但肯定可以买很多学校乐队制服、儿童书籍或儿科医院病房。帕顿的善良总有一种超凡脱俗的特质。就好像你遇到过的最善良的人，突然拥有了数亿美元的现金。但尽管她的贡献是严肃的——对音乐产业，对全国数百万儿童——她从不把自己看得太重，也许这正是她的魅力所在。“我有点沉迷于给予的感觉，”她在2021年告诉《人物》杂志，“知道我在为别人做好事。”而这一点，无论你是否是传奇的千万富翁乡村巨星，我们所有人都可以用来传承她的遗产。更多内容：名人文化 文化 未来完美 慈善 特朗普对加拿大贸易战的离奇根源 用最新的Vox填字游戏放松一下脑筋 人物

readings.title: 6 ways to give that aren’t about money
body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

##段落

6种不花钱的给予方式
2024年1月22日
/
克里斯·安德森
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
Reddit

MINIWIDE / iStock
好消息：你不必写下一堆支票，也能成为一个慷慨的人。事实上，许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨之举，都是量身定制、直击特定需求的时间、精力、才华与爱的馈赠。这种给予方式对所有人都敞开大门。

##段落

许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨之举，都是量身定制、直击特定需求的时间、精力、才华与爱的馈赠。
不知道从哪里开始？以下是六种时间与关注力的馈赠方式，它们有巨大潜力激发出影响数百万人的涟漪效应，选自TED负责人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。

##段落

1. 转移关注
禅宗大师一行禅师教导说，关注是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。慷慨由此开始——愿意停止关注自己，转而关注他人及其需求。从这种联结的行为出发，一切皆有可能。

##段落

事实上，这并不容易。我们大部分时间都迷失在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿去关注他人正在处理的问题。于是我们竖起盾牌。这意味着，许多真正需要我们去关注的人，从未感受到被我们看见。因此，关注的慷慨，就是愿意让自己稍微不舒服、卸下那些盾牌、放弃一些时间、冒险去在意他人的慷慨。

##段落

无论你是停下来与一个需要帮助的人建立有意义的联结，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的议题，你都已经开始了自己的慷慨之旅。

##段落

2. 架设桥梁
在我们这个互联的时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端都在线上公开上演。大量观众可能会紧盯网络骂战不放。如果我们能为更多这样的冲突带来令人满意的解决，会怎样？

##段落

主动接触批评者很难。这是慷慨心态中极具挑战性的一种形式。你是在为了促进人们团结的更大善益而牺牲个人的舒适感。但如果你成功了，会有一个强大的连锁收益：你在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。这是给我们所有人的礼物。

##段落

我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能够解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。

##段落

3. 分享知识
在无数情境中，我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能够解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。
我们给某人最重要的建议是——

在TED舞台上发言，最根本的心态不是把演讲当作推销（无论是推销事业还是某项事业），而是将其视为一份礼物。这是一个与听众自由分享宝贵想法的机会，而这些想法有可能在未来多年中影响听众的生活。
如果你拥有他人可能受益的知识，不妨思考如何分享它，以产生涟漪效应。你花几个小时准备和行动的事情，可能会点亮某人的生活——而这或许只是开始。
4. 促成连接
在我们这个互联的时代，我们所能触及的人脉网络比以往任何时候都更重要。因此，病毒式慷慨最重要的形式之一，就是帮助人们与他人建立联系。最简单的做法就是进行引荐。
正如心理学家兼TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所言，引荐对给予者来说相当容易，而对接受者来说却价值连城。问问许多人他们是如何遇见伴侣、获得理想工作或找到创意项目的完美合作伙伴的，答案往往相同：有人——朋友、邻居或同事——将他们介绍给了对的人。你实际上是在给予他人进入你资源网络的通道，而这些引荐可能产生指数级的后果。
5. 展现好客
在人类学家唐纳德·布朗的杰出著作《人类共相》中，他记录了热情好客是如何成为在每一种被研究过的文化中都能观察到的数百种人类行为之一。但如果好客如此普遍（且如此愉悦），它真的算是一种慷慨吗？嗯，是的。撇开任何成本不谈，邀请某人来家里——无论是朋友还是潜在的新朋友——都需要付出努力。只看你正在追的下一集剧集要容易得多。
那么，好客如何促成感染式慷慨呢？好客触及我们与他人建立联系的最深层本能，而每一次好客体验都会唤起回报的渴望。
人们当然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健，但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑和超越——这些都是迷醉的元素。
6. 创造迷醉
先锋艺术家莉莉·叶被舞蹈家兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔邀请，在她家乡费城一块荒废废弃的土地上开展一个社区艺术项目。“我感兴趣但完全害怕，”叶回忆道，“我资源匮乏，也没有在社区环境户外工作的经验。我想逃跑，但我不想在镜子里看到懦夫。所以我走进了项目。”
这个社区项目演变成了“艺术与人文之村”，一个充满由当地成年人创作的树木、雕塑和马赛克作品的艺术公园。

##段落  
与叶合作的老年人和儿童。叶的工作让她深刻认识到：在公共空间创造美，对社区具有深远的疗愈和变革力量。

##段落  
人们当然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑和超越——这些都是“魅力”的元素。那些能够带来魅力的人，能赠予一份无比珍贵的礼物。

##段落

readings.title: Sharing meals can reduce your risk of depression
body: 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google David Robson and Alessia Franco Commensality – the act of sharing meals – can reduce your risk of depression and dementia. It sounds almost too good to be true, but one simple change to your eating habits could do wonders for your body and brain. It can reduce your risk of depression and protect you from dementia. It can increase the pleasure you take in your food, and perhaps even cause you to live longer. We're not talking about a new fad diet, but one of humanity's most ancient practices: commensality, or the act of eating with others. "The sharing of meals is an essential mechanism for bonding and building trust and connecting with others," says Jan-Emmanuel De Neve, a professor of economics and behavioural science as the University of Oxford. And that has serious repercussions for our wellbeing. Sadly, the increased isolation of the modern world is making this increasingly unusual. But it might be easier than you'd think to reach out to others and harness the ancient connection between food and friendship. Much of the research on commensality has focused on its consequences for our mental health. One study, by Xinyi Wang and colleagues at the Zhejiang Provincial Centre for Disease Control and Prevention in China, involved surveying 9,361 women aged 60 and over. It found that the number of people sitting around the table at mealtimes was a clear predictor of someone's risk of depression . This remained the case even after the team had controlled for a host of other factors that are known to influence people's wellbeing, such as their general health and wealth, and whether or not that person lived alone. This, the team concluded, suggests that there was something unique about commensality that affects our mental health. Many other studies point to the same conclusions. Researchers from Tokyo, for instance, found that people aged 65-74 who lived with their families, yet ate alone, had five times the odds of developing depressive symptoms than those who regularly ate in company .  Arguably the strongest evidence comes from the World Happiness Report – a yearly analysis of wellbeing based on a global survey from the opinion polling company Gallup. In 2024, the company was sponsored by the Japanese food manufacturer Ajinomoto to add a section on people's eating habits, which included the following questions:  Thinking about the last 7 days … (1) On how many days did you eat lunch with someone you know? (2) On how many days did you eat dinner with someone you know?"  "My eyes lit up when I saw," De Neve says, who co-authored a chapter on the importance of commensality in the latest World Happiness Report. "We're looking at about 150,000 individuals around the world who responded to that question."  De Neve's team found that the more meals that people shared with others, the higher they scored on standard measures of emotional wellbeing, with quite astonishing consistency. "It was as predictive of someone's life satisfaction as their employment status and your relative income," he says – two factors that are known to be enormously important for wellbeing.    De Neve emphasises that the questions about meal sharing may simply serve as a "proxy" of someone's general social life – but he suspects there is something special about eating together. He points out that the English word companion comes from the Latin roots cum and pānis – "with bread" – while Chinese term 伙伴 ( huǒ bàn ) for the same concept derives from characters describing a military unit sharing the same kitchen stove. "It has deep cultural roots," he says.  In his book Friends, Robin Dunbar – a biological anthropologist at the University of Oxford – suggests that eating naturally triggers the endorphin system, those feel-good chemicals behind our natural highs. This could strengthen the bond forged over a meal, leading us to feel a heightened sense of connection. In 2025, Japanese researchers found that people who regularly eat alone have reduced brain volume in key regions associated with cognitive function Intriguingly, the presence of other people may amplify the pleasure of the food itself . One series of studies by Erica Boothby at the University of Pennsylvania found that people eating chocolate in another person's company found it considerably tastier.    Eating together may even slow the brain's ageing.  In 2025, Japanese researchers found that people who regularly eat alone have reduced brain volume in key regions associated with cognitive function, including the medial temporal lobe and the hippocampus. Although some of these differences appeared to be linked to the diet itself – in general, people who eat by themselves tend to consume less nutritious foods – it could not account for everything, suggesting that the reduced social connection was also playing a role in their long-term brain health.  The authors speculated the enjoyment and enhanced social support of the shared meals could soothe stress, which is a known risk factor for neural decline. Alternatively, the conversations over the meals could provide extra mental stimulation that keeps our brains active into old age. The participants were considered to have normal cognitive function during the study, but the researchers warned that this neural decline could eventually predispose them to dementia. The World Happiness Report noted that eating practices vary widely between countries, and we may learn a lot from one nation's efforts to preserve its culture of conviviality. On average, the Japanese share fewer than four meals together each week. In the UK and US, that figure is around seven to eight, while in Italy, it approaches nine. Italy is, of course, well known for its sociable food culture. When Unesco awarded Italian cuisine the status of an Intangible Cultural Heritage, the organisation highlighted the crucial role that meals play in "connecting with family and the community, whether at home, in schools, or through festivals, ceremonies and social gatherings". It may be no surprise, therefore, that the country is also leading the way in finding ways to protect its culture of commensality against the pressures of the modern world. The Slow Food Movement , which originated in Italy, was launched 50 years ago as a direct reaction to the growing popularity of fast food. It is perhaps best known for its aims to protect local traditions and encourage sustainable consumption, but the movement has long emphasised the importance of centring our days around shared meals. "In Italy, sharing food is a philosophy in its own right: to cook together and share the preparation of what we put on the table," explains Barbara Nappini, the president of Slow Food Italia. "This requires care and patience."   Even so, the pressures of the 21st Century have led many Italians to feel increasingly isolated. But if you don't want to eat alone, the solution might be easier than you think. You may already be surrounded by people who would jump at the chance of sharing a meal with you. A whole body of literature shows that people are far more receptive to these kinds of invitations than we expect . In general, we underestimate how much people like us enjoy our company and want to spend time with us. So if you know someone who might also be feeling lonely and could appreciate the chance for a conversation over some good food, the best solution is just to ask them. More like this: • Why you eat more when you're in company • How chewing more boosts your brain • The key to losing weight may be enjoying your food And if you’re really struggling to think of someone, there are technological solutions. In 2019, the Italian tech entrepreneur Paolo Bavaro founded the app Tablo to connect lonely diners. It has so far been used more than 300,000 times. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the average user is young – around 30 years old. "At that age, it's harder to make friends," says Bavaro. "You work a lot, many of your friends have families – you want to socialise but you don't know who to go out with." Bavaro's app, he emphasises, isn't aimed at a particular "type" of person, and it shouldn't be considered a dating app – the aim is to enlarge people's social circle at a time of life when they most need it.  When we mentioned the app to De Neve, he pointed us to an experiment by psychologist Jamil Zaki at Stanford University, who helped set-up " platonic dates " for shy students to meet up at the campus coffee shop – an initiative that helped enhance their social confidence. Such interventions, he suggests, can "have quite long-lasting benefits".  By breaking bread, you may just build a lasting friendship, and enhance your health and happiness in the process. * David Robson is an award-winning science writer and author. His latest book is The Laws of Connection: 13 Social Strategies That Will Transform Your Life . He is @d_a_robson on Twitter and @davidarobson on Instagram and Threads. ** Alessia Franco is an author and a journalist focusing on history, culture, society, storytelling and its effects on people. She is La Raccontatrice on Facebook and @la_raccontatrice on Instagram  -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . 两天前 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 大卫·罗布森和亚历西娅·弗兰科 共食——即与他人共享餐食的行为——可以降低你患抑郁症和痴呆症的风险。这听起来几乎好得令人难以置信，但对你饮食习惯的一个简单改变，就能为你的身体和大脑带来奇效。它可以降低你患抑郁症的风险，并保护你免受痴呆症的困扰。它可以增加你从食物中获得的愉悦感，甚至可能让你活得更久。我们谈论的不是一种新的时尚饮食，而是人类最古老的习惯之一：共食，即与他人一起进食的行为。“共享餐食是建立纽带、培养信任以及与他人联结的重要机制，”牛津大学经济学和行为科学教授扬-伊曼纽尔·德·内夫说。而这对我们的幸福感有着深远的影响。遗憾的是，现代世界日益加剧的孤立感正使这种行为变得越来越不寻常。但与他人建立联系并利用食物与友谊之间的古老纽带，可能比你想象的要容易。关于共食的研究大多集中在其对我们心理健康的影响上。中国浙江省疾病预防控制中心的王欣怡及其同事进行的一项研究，调查了9361名60岁及以上的女性。研究发现，用餐时围坐在餐桌旁的人数，是预测一个人抑郁症风险的明确指标。即使在团队控制了已知会影响人们幸福感的一系列其他因素（如总体健康状况、财富以及是否独居）之后，这一结论依然成立。该团队由此得出结论，这表明共食中存在着某种独特的东西，会影响我们的心理健康。许多其他研究也得出了相同的结论。例如，来自东京的研究人员发现，65-74岁与家人同住但独自进食的人，患上抑郁症状的几率是那些经常与他人共餐者的五倍。可以说，最有力的证据来自《世界幸福报告》——这是一项基于民调公司盖洛普全球调查的年度幸福感分析。2024年，日本食品制造商味之素赞助该公司增加了一个关于人们饮食习惯的板块，其中包括以下问题：回想过去7天……（1）你有几天与认识的人共进午餐？（2）你有几天与认识的人共进晚餐？“我看到这些时眼睛一亮，”德·内夫说，他合著了最新《世界幸福报告》中关于共食重要性的一个章节。“我们正在研究全球约15万名回答了该问题的个体。”德·

维的研究团队发现，人们与他人共享的餐食次数越多，他们在标准情绪健康测量中的得分就越高，且这种一致性令人震惊。他说：“这对其生活满意度的预测力，与就业状况和相对收入相当”——而这两者已知对幸福感极为重要。德·内夫强调，关于共享餐食的问题可能仅仅是作为某人整体社交生活的“代理指标”——但他怀疑共同进餐本身具有某种特殊之处。他指出，英语单词“companion”源自拉丁语词根“cum”和“pānis”——意为“与面包”——而中文中表达相同概念的“伙伴”一词，则源于描述共享同一灶台的军事单位的字符。他说：“这具有深厚的文化根源。”在其著作《朋友》中，牛津大学生物人类学家罗宾·邓巴提出，进食自然触发内啡肽系统，这些是带来自然快感的愉悦化学物质。这可能加强餐桌上建立的纽带，让我们感受到更强烈的联系感。2025年，日本研究人员发现，经常独自进食的人在与认知功能相关的关键脑区（包括内侧颞叶和海马体）中，脑容量有所减少。尽管其中一些差异似乎与饮食本身有关——通常，独自进食者倾向于摄入营养较少的食物——但这无法解释所有现象，表明减少的社交联系也在其长期脑健康中发挥作用。作者推测，共享餐食带来的愉悦感和增强的社会支持可能缓解压力，而压力是神经衰退的已知风险因素。或者，餐桌上的对话可能提供额外的脑力刺激，使大脑在老年时保持活跃。研究期间，参与者被认为具有正常认知功能，但研究人员警告，这种神经衰退最终可能使他们易患痴呆症。世界幸福报告指出，各国饮食习惯差异很大，我们可以从一个国家努力维护其欢聚文化中学到很多。平均而言，日本人共享的餐食次数少于四次……

每周人们会聚在一起。在英国和美国，这一数字约为七到八次，而在意大利则接近九次。意大利当然以其社交性的饮食文化而闻名。当联合国教科文组织将意大利美食列为非物质文化遗产时，该组织强调了餐食在“与家庭和社区建立联系”中的关键作用，无论是在家中、学校，还是通过节日、仪式和社交聚会。因此，这个国家在寻找保护其共餐文化免受现代世界压力方面走在前列，也就不足为奇了。起源于意大利的慢食运动，在50年前发起，直接回应了快餐日益普及的现象。它或许最以保护地方传统和鼓励可持续消费为目标而闻名，但该运动长期以来一直强调将共享餐食作为日常生活中心的重要性。“在意大利，分享食物本身就是一种哲学：一起烹饪，共同准备摆上餐桌的食物，”慢食意大利协会主席芭芭拉·纳皮尼解释道。“这需要关怀和耐心。”即便如此，21世纪的压力导致许多意大利人感到越来越孤立。但如果你不想独自用餐，解决方案可能比你想象的更简单。你周围可能已经有人渴望与你共进一餐。大量文献表明，人们对这类邀请的接受程度远超我们的预期。总的来说，我们低估了别人有多喜欢我们的陪伴，以及他们多么想与我们共度时光。所以，如果你认识某人可能也感到孤独，并且会珍惜在美食陪伴下交谈的机会，最好的解决方案就是直接邀请他们。更多类似内容：• 为什么你在有人陪伴时吃得更多 • 多咀嚼如何促进大脑 • 减肥的关键可能是享受食物如果你实在想不出合适的人选，还有技术解决方案。2019年，意大利科技企业家保罗·巴瓦罗创立了Tablo应用，旨在连接孤独的用餐者。迄今为止，该应用已被使用超过30万次。也许不足为奇的是，平均用户年龄较年轻——大约30岁。“在那个年龄，交朋友更难，”巴瓦罗说。“你工作很多，许多朋友都有家庭——你想社交，但不知道和谁出去。”他强调，他的应用并非针对特定“类型”的人，也不应被视为约会应用——其目的是在人们最需要的时候扩大他们的社交圈。当我们向德·内夫提到这款应用时，他指向了斯坦福大学心理学家贾米尔·扎基进行的一项实验。

该大学的一位研究人员帮助害羞的学生在校园咖啡店安排“柏拉图式约会”，这一举措有助于增强他们的社交信心。他表示，这类干预措施可以“产生相当持久的益处”。通过共进一餐，你或许能建立长久的友谊，并在此过程中增进健康与幸福。* 大卫·罗布森是一位屡获殊荣的科学作家和作者。他的最新著作是《连接的法则：改变你生活的13种社交策略》。他在推特上是@d_a_robson，在Instagram和Threads上是@davidarobson。** 阿莱西娅·弗兰科是一位作者和记者，专注于历史、文化、社会、叙事及其对人们的影响。她在Facebook上是La Raccontatrice，在Instagram上是@la_raccontatrice。-- 如需获取关于健康和福祉的可靠见解，请订阅资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆撰写的《健康修复》通讯，她还撰写了《活得更久更好》和《平静六步法》课程。如需更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境和健康故事，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。心理学 健康 营养 生物学 科学 专题
